tldr: We developed an autonomous AI experimental system that handles circuit design, PCB printing, component placement, real-time testing, and data-driven redesign from a single natural-language prompt without any human intervention.
hero_caption: JARVIS's physical bench environment (a) and the digital twin autonomously constructed from the robot arm's scan (b). Unmodified off-the-shelf equipment (PCB printer, pick-and-place machine, HIL simulator, etc.) is placed as-is, faithfully replicating fixtures and the arm's workspace.
overview:
Hardware development in power electronics relies heavily on iterative cycles of design, prototyping, testing, and refinement. Traditionally, most of this cycle depends on manual human labor—moving boards, swapping tools, wiring, and interpreting measurement data—creating a major bottleneck in development speed. While LLM-based circuit design aids and robotic self-driving laboratories exist, they remain limited to optimizing parameters for fixed chemical recipes and have not achieved a closed loop that designs, manufactures, and evaluates brand-new physical circuit hardware from scratch.

To bridge this gap, the authors developed JARVIS, an embodied agent that autonomously executes every stage of physical hardware development. JARVIS operates standard commercial machines—a robotic arm, a desktop PCB printer, a pick-and-place machine, and a Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL) real-time simulator—without any hardware or firmware modifications. Using a wrist-mounted 3D scanner on the robot arm, it captures the entire workbench to autonomously build an "executable digital twin." Before touching any physical material, JARVIS thoroughly rehearses arm trajectories, thermal expansion, heating times, and circuit behaviors inside the twin.

As a benchmark, when asked in a single sentence on a screen to build a "60 Hz notch filter board for a power converter sensing chain," JARVIS completed circuit design, board printing, component assembly, reflow, real-time HIL testing, and board ejection in 2 hours and 39 minutes. It autonomously recovered from mid-process machine errors, deduced the cause of discrepancies in measured frequency response (low-frequency gain droop caused by instrument input loading), and generated and rehearsed an improved next-generation KiCad design entirely on its own.
contributions: Demonstrated the first agent system to close the complete physical hardware loop—design, build, test, and learn (redesign)—for circuit boards without human intervention.
Built an "executable digital twin" that automatically places CAD models from robot arm scan data to pre-run real machine control code alongside multi-physics simulations.
Established embodied manipulation techniques operating unmodified off-the-shelf machines through GUI automation and autonomous robotic tool-head changes.

Implemented a highly reliable, auditable autonomous operating framework combining self-verification mechanisms, an attempt ledger tracking intent and provenance for every action, and dual-screen visualization.

sections.heading: Freeing Circuit Hardware Development from Human Hands
sections.summary: Power electronics board development relies on a design-build-test-improve loop, yet physical steps have always required manual human work. JARVIS is the first agent to run this entire loop completely autonomously from natural language requests.
sections.details:
Power electronics underpins modern energy infrastructure, from power grids and electric vehicles to data centers. Developing these systems demands repeated cycles of requirement definition, circuit design, PCB prototyping, and Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL) testing against real-time simulators. However, all the physical steps—moving boards between machines, changing tools, wiring, and interpreting results—have remained strictly manual.

While self-driving laboratories have made great strides in chemistry and materials discovery, most focus on parameter optimization over fixed procedures, such as varying liquid dispensation volumes. Circuit hardware development requires printing distinct traces, dispensing different pastes, mounting varied components, and applying customized test sequences for each new design, which traditional automation cannot handle.

JARVIS tackles this challenge across four stages:
- Learning the specifications, limits, and proven procedures/pitfalls of each machine.
- Scanning the bench with a wrist-mounted 3D scanner to autonomously build an executable digital twin where the real control code runs directly.
- Designing circuits and boards from natural language and rehearsing the entire process—including thermal, kinematic, and electrical behavior—inside the twin.
- Directly operating the physical PCB printer, pick-and-place machine, and HIL simulator via the robot arm and agent to manufacture, measure, and derive improved designs.

In a demonstration building a 60 Hz notch filter used in grid-connected inverters, the agent completed the board in 2 hours and 39 minutes with 50.6 dB attenuation after a human entered just a single sentence to approve the plan.

sections.heading: Moving from Fixed Recipes to Autonomous Device Creation
sections.summary: Compared to prior work in self-driving labs and LLM circuit design, JARVIS is the only system integrating direct control of unmodified commercial tools, 3D-scan-based twin generation, and physical feedback from real hardware testing.
sections.details:
Related work spans five major areas:

### Self-Driving Laboratories
In chemistry and materials science, combining robotics with Bayesian optimization to automate photocatalyst discovery or chemical synthesis is an active field. However, these systems primarily vary volumes or temperatures within predefined procedures. In contrast, JARVIS designs physically unique circuit boards from scratch and generates the machine control programs anew for each run.

### LLM Agents for Science and Robotics
Researchers have explored language models for experimental planning, language-conditioned robotic grasping/assembly, and automated optical bench alignment. JARVIS pushes this further by unifying the complete sequence across multiple manufacturing tools and measurement instruments under a single agent.

### Language Models for Electronics and Power Electronics
LLMs are emerging for HDL code generation, analog circuit design, and power electronics modulation schemes. However, these efforts have remained confined to software simulation, leaving physical manufacturing to humans. JARVIS closes the loop by physically printing, assembling, and testing real boards on real-time simulators.

### Digital Twins and Real-to-Sim
Scanning real environments to build simulation setups is gaining traction in robotics. JARVIS's twin is unique because it is built autonomously from robot scans without human modeling, and it executes the exact control code, thermal models, and circuit physics used on physical machines.

sections.heading: Operating Unmodified Commercial Machines Like a Skilled Technician
sections.summary: Powered by Claude Opus 5.5, JARVIS coordinates an off-the-shelf robot arm, PCB printer, pick-and-place machine, and HIL simulator without any hardware modifications. Self-verification and rigorous safety controls ensure safe, fully autonomous operation.
sections.details:
The system comprises four core layers: the Agent, the Executable Digital Twin, the Accountable Execution Layer, and the Physical Bench.

### III-A Physical Bench Setup
The bench features standard commercial hardware: a 6-axis collaborative robot arm with a wrist-mounted camera and 3D scanner, a desktop PCB printer dispensing conductive silver ink and solder paste, a pick-and-place machine with two vision cameras, an OPAL-RT HIL real-time simulator, and an oscilloscope for verification. None of these machines have undergone hardware or firmware modifications.

### III-B Board Handling: Custom Carrier System
Boards are transported inside a two-piece carrier consisting of a base and an adapter. The robot arm moves the entire carrier between machines, and the assembly withstands the PCB printer's heated bed. After testing, the adapter is pressed against push-out pins on the bench, ejecting the finished board from below so a fresh substrate can be clicked into place.

### III-C Agent and Machine Knowledge Management
JARVIS is powered by Claude Opus 5.5. For each machine, it maintains text ledgers detailing "Facts" (configurations and safety bounds), "Proven procedures" (validated operational sequences), and "Known pitfalls" (past failures and mitigations). Long-term memory is preserved across sessions through structured files.

### III-D Operating Unmodified Machines
This is the most pragmatic and demanding aspect of the system:
- **Autonomous Tool Changes by the Arm**: Although the PCB printer was designed for manual tool swaps, the arm executes the manufacturer's exact mechanical steps to dock and undock probes, ink heads, and paste heads (eight tool changes per board).
- **Direct GUI Manipulation**: Rather than modifying proprietary printer software, the agent visually inspects UI button labels and states to click and control the interface like a human.
- **Adapting to Board Warpage**: Raw substrates are rarely perfectly flat. Before printing, the agent maps surface elevation using a touch probe and adjusts nozzle heights dynamically. It also relaxes probe step thresholds post-printing to account for ink thickness.
- **Coordinating the Pick-and-Place and Simulator**: The agent scripts the open-source pick-and-place software while maintaining software interlocks to verify safety (head parked, nozzle raised) before the arm enters. It also auto-builds and deploys custom test models on the simulator.

### III-E to G Self-Verification, Accountability, and Safety
To eliminate human visual inspection, JARVIS verifies every step using the 3D scanner, onboard cameras, and sensors. Every physical action is logged in an "Attempt ledger" documenting intent, plan, expected outcome, result, and lessons learned, with provenance tags attached to every fact. Robot speeds, heated bed temperatures/times, and keep-out boxes are strictly enforced in software.

sections.heading: Self-Building an Executable Digital Twin from 3D Scans
sections.summary: Using its wrist scanner, the arm scans the workbench to construct a twin by aligning point cloud panoramas with CAD models. This twin simulates not just geometry, but motion planning, thermal dynamics, timing, and circuit physics using real machine code.
sections.details:
Rather than being manually crafted by a modeling team, JARVIS's digital twin is self-constructed and updated directly by the agent, making it both self-building and executable.

### IV-A Constructing the Twin from Scans
The robot sweeps its wrist-mounted 3D scanner across the bench from multiple angles. Because the arm's pose is precisely known, scans are merged into a single registered point-cloud panorama in the arm's frame (27 viewpoints, ~1.17 million points).
However, raw scans suffer from occlusions on the undersides and backs of machines. The agent bridges this by automatically fitting pre-stored, complete CAD models of each tool and fixture to the scan data, producing an occlusion-free 3D model of the bench without human assistance.

### IV-B The Four Layers of the Twin
The twin extends far beyond visual rendering through four distinct layers:
- **Geometry**: Accurate spatial placement of CAD models, used for collision avoidance and arm reachability analysis.
- **Behavior**: Simulates the exact trajectory generators, inverse kinematics, collision checkers, and machine interlock states used on the physical hardware.
- **Physics**: Predicts heat transfer from the bed to the substrate (setting curing/reflow temperature profiles and thermal expansion stresses on fixtures), calculates step durations, solves circuit equations under component tolerances and instrument loads, and models measurement calibration.
- **Provenance**: Tracks the origin of every value in the twin—tagging it as measured, CAD-derived, simulated, or assumed, along with cryptographic hashes—to clarify how much empirical trust backs each parameter.

sections.heading: Translating Prompts to Code and Virtual Rehearsals
sections.summary: Starting from a natural language request for a power-line noise notch filter, JARVIS generates acceptance code and circuit schematics. It rehearses the full 42-step sequence in the twin, catching design and planning flaws before running physical machines.
sections.details:
### V-A From Need to Acceptance Code
Upon receiving natural language instructions, the agent converts the requirements into quantitative acceptance criteria:
- Notch frequency (point of minimum gain) within $60\pm 1$ Hz
- Attenuation at 60.0 Hz $\le -40$ dB
- Flat passbands (gain within $0\pm 0.6$ dB at 1 Hz and 10 kHz)
- Agreement with design theory ($-3$ dB corner frequencies within 10% of theoretical values)

The agent writes the executable Python acceptance code to evaluate these criteria automatically.

### V-B Circuit Design and Automated Layout
JARVIS chose a passive twin-T notch filter architecture consisting of resistors $R, R, R/2$ and capacitors $C, C, 2C$. By selecting four $R=26.4\text{ k}\Omega$ (0.1% precision) resistors and four $C=100\text{ nF}$ (1% precision) capacitors, it produced half- and double-values via parallel pairs. A 300-run Monte Carlo simulation confirmed that all tolerance variations maintained 60 Hz attenuation below $-43$ dB.

Next, it simultaneously generated the KiCad PCB layout, printer toolpaths, pick-and-place job files, and simulator models. To eliminate drilling, all parts were surface-mount devices (SMD), supplemented by three fiducial markers for the pick-and-place camera and six test pads topped with gold discs for probe contact.

### V-C 42-Step Rehearsal in the Twin
The manufacturing and testing process was compiled into a 42-step sequence and executed end-to-end inside the digital twin. This verified arm reachability, bed cooling durations, and frequency-sweep signal levels.
Rehearsal caught five critical issues before any material was consumed, including an ink priming pattern that intersected the functional circuit traces and an overly coarse frequency sweep that would have falsely failed a valid board.

sections.heading: From Physical Build to Real-Time Testing and Redesign
sections.summary: Following human sign-off, JARVIS autonomously printed, cured, pasted, placed, reflowed, tested, and exchanged the board. By analyzing measured frequency response against theory, it identified discrepancies and drafted an improved next-generation design.
sections.details:
### VI-A The Manufacturing Sequence
1. **Bench Scan**: The agent re-scans the bench to verify that fixtures and tools match the twin.
2. **Height Mapping**: With the touch probe mounted, the arm measures substrate warpage across multiple points.
3. **Trace Printing and Curing**: Silver nanoparticle ink is dispensed, followed by thermal curing on the heated bed at 240 °C for 12 minutes. While cooling, probe tolerances are automatically relaxed to account for trace height.
4. **Solder Paste Dispensing**: Low-temperature tin-bismuth (Sn-Bi, 138 °C melting point) paste is deposited onto component pads.
5. **Part Assembly**: The carrier enters the pick-and-place machine, which uses vision alignment to mount 14 parts (resistors, capacitors, and gold probe discs).
6. **Reflow**: The board returns to the heated bed for a 2-minute reflow cycle to solder connections.

### VI-B Testing and Cross-Instrument Verification
The assembled board is transferred to the test station, where the arm lowers a spring-loaded test head onto the pads. The OPAL-RT simulator injects a 1 V sinusoidal sweep from 1 Hz to 10 kHz to measure complex gain, using fine 0.25 Hz steps around the notch (57–64 Hz). An oscilloscope independently records the signals to cross-validate results across two instruments.

### VI-C Automated Board Exchange
Once testing concludes, the arm presses the carrier onto the bench's push-out pin to eject the finished board and installs a fresh blank substrate into the adapter, immediately preparing for the next run.

### VI-D Learning from Data and Closing the Loop
Beyond binary pass/fail checks, the agent physically reasoned why the measured frequency response deviated from ideal theory. By fitting circuit models to empirical data, JARVIS concluded that the passband gain drop near 1 Hz stemmed from instrument input impedance loading and substrate leakage. It then designed a second-generation circuit in KiCad that lowered impedance by 10× (resistors reduced by 10×, capacitors increased by 10×) to resist loading, and verified the fix in the twin.

### VI-E Dual-Screen Visualization
A large "Live display" in the lab showed real-time twin status and machine telemetry, while a compact "Thinking screen" streamed the agent's natural-language reasoning logs.

captions.F10: The dual-screen interface observed during experiments: (a) the Live Display showing real-time machine states and the digital twin, and (b) the Thinking Screen displaying the agent's internal reasoning process.

sections.heading: First-Time-Right Autonomy: Notch Board Built in 2 h 39 min
sections.summary: JARVIS completed all 42 steps in 2 hours and 39 minutes without human intervention, achieving 50.6 dB attenuation at 60 Hz. It recovered from hardware hiccups, identified the cause of measurement discrepancies, and generated an improved next design.
sections.details:
The experimental validation evaluated four core research questions (Q1–Q4):

### Q1: Did it run without human assistance?
After an initial one-sentence confirmation from a human ("Plan looks good, proceed"), **zero human physical or software intervention occurred**. JARVIS executed all 42 steps in 2 hours and 39 minutes. Robot motion accounted for 33 minutes, while heating and cooling took 93 minutes.
When physical issues arose—such as tool-head electrical contact errors and a frozen printer GUI—the agent recovered autonomously by redocking the tool head and verifying position offsets remained within 0.2 mm.

### Q2: Did the board meet specifications?
The fabricated board exhibited a notch frequency of 60.29 Hz (target: 60 Hz) and 50.6 dB attenuation (target: $\ge 40$ dB). Corner frequencies matched design theory within 4.0%, validating fabrication precision. However, passband gain at 1 Hz was $-1.29$ dB, slightly missing the flatness criterion (within $-0.6$ dB). Simulator and oscilloscope measurements matched closely within 0.05 dB across the passband.

### Q3: What did it learn, and how did it improve the design?
Investigating the 1 Hz gain droop, the agent ruled out component tolerance error and solder defects, determining that instrument input impedance loaded the filter's output. Model fitting identified an effective load of ~340 $\text{k}\Omega$. JARVIS generated a revised KiCad design scaling resistors down by 10× ($2.64\text{ k}\Omega$) and capacitors up by 10× ($1\mu\text{F}$). Twin simulations showed this would lift 1 Hz gain to $-0.15$ dB, comfortably passing criteria. It also proposed physical process improvements, such as adding a forced-air cooling fan to cut bed wait times.

### Q4: What did digital twin rehearsals prevent?
As detailed in Table IV, pre-run rehearsals caught and resolved five defects. Notably, it prevented a test failure where an overly coarse frequency sweep would have rejected a valid board, and fixed an overlapping trace layout error—all without wasting any physical material.

sections.heading: Digital Twins as World Models for Self-Driving Hardware Labs
sections.summary: This work highlights the power of using digital twins as executable world models, enabling agents to reason over physical causality. Future opportunities include multilayer boards, active circuits, and learning robotic motion policies from execution logs.
sections.details:
### Digital Twins as World Models
Rather than serving merely as visual 3D assets, JARVIS's twin functions as an executable world model running real machine code while concurrently predicting thermal, temporal, and circuit physics. Because every parameter carries provenance, the agent can deliberate inside simulation and evaluate empirical certainty before taking physical actions.

### Reasoning Over Physical Causality
Moving beyond fixed parameter tuning to synthesize novel physical hardware requires deducing why empirical measurements deviate from theory and identifying root physical mechanisms (parasitic capacitance, contact resistance, instrument loading). JARVIS demonstrated this analytical capability much like an experienced engineer.

### Future Horizons
The underlying architecture is agnostic to the notch filter benchmark. By swapping circuit models and acceptance code, the system extends naturally to 50 Hz grid filters, active op-amp stages, and power converter switching topologies. Furthermore, dense execution logs—including joint trajectories and sensor streams—provide high-quality demonstration datasets for robot imitation learning and Sim-to-Real transfer.

sections.heading: A New Era for Autonomous Hardware Development
sections.summary: JARVIS closed the entire design-build-HIL test-redesign loop from natural language prompts. As an embodied agent turning standard workbenches into self-driving laboratories, it points the way toward the future of power electronics and hardware engineering.
sections.details:
JARVIS demonstrates that an embodied agent can close the entire development cycle for physical circuit hardware. From a single natural-language prompt on a screen, boards are designed, printed, assembled on unmodified desktop tools, tested on real-time simulators, and iteratively improved—all without human intervention.

This high level of autonomy rests on four foundational pillars: learning machine limits, building an executable digital twin from 3D scans, conducting exhaustive virtual rehearsals, and executing accountable, self-verifying physical operations.

sections.heading: The Authors' Reflections: The Gap to Expert Intuition
sections.summary: While celebrating the flawless first-time autonomous run, the authors candidly observe that routing choices and impedance oversights resemble the work of a talented novice rather than a seasoned layout master, marking the path forward.
sections.details:
From an electrical and computer engineering perspective, the authors noted that seeing a complete, autonomous run succeed on its very first try while self-resolving hardware anomalies was genuinely striking—human engineers rarely get a complex first build right without manual troubleshooting.

At the same time, they point out that the finished board unmistakably reflects the hand of a capable novice rather than a seasoned layout expert:
- Traces turn at sharp 90-degree angles instead of the 45-degree bevels preferred by experienced designers (negligible at 60 Hz, but poor design practice).
- Some traces take long detours around board edges instead of direct paths.
- The initial design overlooked downstream instrument loading, causing the 1 Hz gain drop.

Experienced engineers avoid these traps instinctively, showing that capturing tacit expert intuition remains an open challenge. The authors view this milestone not as a final destination, but as the first step toward professional-grade autonomous hardware laboratories.

takeaways: Demonstrated that the entire design-build-test-redesign hardware cycle can be fully automated using a robotic arm, an LLM, and unmodified commercial tools.
Proved that self-building an executable digital twin from 3D scans to conduct virtual rehearsals is highly effective at preventing material waste and false test rejections.
Showed that agents can go beyond tuning parameters to reason through discrepancies between measurements and physics models, autonomously synthesizing next-generation schematics and board layouts.
Validated an embodied automation approach where the agent operates human-facing GUIs and swaps tool heads directly, unlocking autonomy without requiring expensive custom laboratory machinery.
limitations: Board layouts exhibit novice routing artifacts, such as 90-degree corners and inefficient trace detours, highlighting the remaining gap in capturing tacit design intuition and aesthetics.

Natural cooling phases following ink sintering and solder reflow accounted for roughly 60% of total run time (93 out of 159 minutes), pointing to the need for hardware additions like forced-air cooling to boost throughput.
The current demonstration is limited to single-layer passive notch filters; extending the framework to double-sided/multilayer boards and active switching power electronics remains future work.
